observation.visible_scene: A turquoise indoor pool viewed through a wet glass pane (scattered water droplets on the lens). Several penguins are at the water surface: a large penguin in the lower-left foreground is seen half-submerged through the waterline with its dark back, white belly and splayed flippers visible; a second penguin swims in the middle of the frame with its head and upper back above the surface; a third penguin's head bobs in the upper-middle background; and a fourth small head floats in the upper-left background. A pale pool wall runs along the top-right edge.
visible_changes: The foreground penguin's flippers shift from a wide-spread paddle posture (early frames) to a more folded, trailing position (later frames), while its body drifts slowly toward the left edge of the frame.

The middle penguin continuously paddles: its head rises and dips, its body rotates slightly, and it translates gradually rightward relative to the frame, with ripples and splash forming around its neck.
The two background penguin heads bob up and down and the upper-left one moves slowly to the right.
The visible waterline tilts more steeply from left to right over the clip, and the droplet pattern on the glass shifts slightly, indicating surface sloshing and/or small camera movement.
No penguin fully submerges or leaves the frame during the excerpt; all remain at the surface throughout.
outside_clip_unknowns: The clip is a temporal crop; the penguins' positions before t=0 and after the last frame are unknown, and it is not shown whether any dive or exit.
Whether the glass is a viewing window or a barrier, and what is on the other side, is not established.
The cause of the waterline tilt change (camera tilt vs. wave) cannot be determined from these frames alone.
uncertain_details: It is unclear how much of the apparent leftward/rightward drift is true penguin translation versus camera pan/tilt, since the background wall and droplets move inconsistently with a single rigid camera.
The exact number of penguins is hard to confirm because reflections and partial submersion blur some bodies; at least four heads are distinguishable.
Flipper motion is partly obscured by refraction at the waterline, so the precise stroke cycle cannot be resolved.
